title: XI. Object is the coherent biblical text; Hebrew and Greek authentic norms
pass_a_gloss: Pass A clause gloss: Glassius demonstrates this at length in Sacred Philology, Book 1, tracts 1 plus 2. The Greek text belonging toward that New Testament, preserved in approved codices, stands as likewise so free from corruptions that it stands as that most exact norm by which all versions plus interpretations ought toward be examined plus corrected. Further: that Hebrew text belonging toward that Old Testament, furnished plus corrected with Masoretic notes as preserved by us Christians in approved copies (even Jewish ones), stands as so free from all corruption — whether belonging toward diction plus sentences or belonging toward letters plus points — that it stands as that divine NORM, canon, plus rule by which all versions in other tongues, plus especially that Latin Vulgate, ought toward be examined and emended. Sense stands as drawn from that nature and order belonging toward that words as they regard one another in Scripture's sayings, and stands as perfected by the Holy Spirit alone — whose alone stands as true interpretation, just as in civil law the interpretation belonging toward statutes belongs to him who constituted them. The former belongs to whole utterances; the latter to single words. Sense stands as one thing, signification another. Clement belonging to Alexandria (Stromata 7) calls the text the body and fabric belonging to God's prophecy, in which, as subject-matter, words stand as considered, and in the words a proper or tropical signification, from which the sense is so drawn that the interpreter permits neither himself to be severed from the text, nor words from the text, nor sense from the words. The object is the biblical text cohering with itself in its whole series. XI.
pass_b_english: XI. The object is the biblical text cohering with itself in its whole series. Clement of Alexandria (Stromata 7) calls the text the body and fabric of God's prophecy, in which, as subject-matter, words are considered, and in the words a proper or tropical signification, from which the sense is so drawn that the interpreter permits neither himself to be severed from the text, nor words from the text, nor sense from the words. Sense is one thing, signification another. The former belongs to whole utterances; the latter to single words. Sense is drawn from the nature and order of the words as they regard one another in Scripture's sayings, and is perfected by the Holy Spirit alone — whose alone is true interpretation, just as in civil law the interpretation of statutes belongs to him who constituted them.

Further: the Hebrew text of the Old Testament, furnished and corrected with Masoretic notes as preserved by us Christians in approved copies (even Jewish ones), is so free from all corruption — whether of diction and sentences or of letters and points — that it is the divine NORM, canon, and rule by which all versions in other tongues, and especially the Latin Vulgate, ought to be examined and emended. The Greek text of the New Testament, preserved in approved codices, is likewise so free from corruptions that it is the most exact norm by which all versions and interpretations ought to be examined and corrected. Glassius demonstrates this at length in Sacred Philology, Book 1, tracts 1 and 2.
source_text: XI. Objectum est textus Biblicus tota secum serie cohaerens. Clemens Alexandrinus lib.7. Strom. textum appellat to soma tes tou Theou propheteias, corpus & telam prophetiae, in qua, tanquam subjecta materia, considerantur verba, in verbis significatus proprius aut tropicus, ex quibus sensus ita elicitur, ut interpres neque se a textu, neque a textu verba, neque a verbis sensum separari permittat. Aliud vero est sensus, aliud significatus. Ille dictorum integratorum est, hic verborum singulorum. Ille ex horum natura & ordine, quo se in dictis Scripturae respiciunt, elicitur, & a Spiritu sancto perficitur, cujus solius interpretatio vera est, sicut & in civilibus juris legumque constitutionibus earum interpretatio ad eum pertinet, qui eas constituit. Caeterum, textus Hebraicus V.T. notis Masoreticis instructus & correctus, prout a nobis Christianis in probatis, etiam Judaicis, exemplaribus asservatur, usurpatur: tum ratione dictionum & sententiarum, tum ratione elementorum, sive literae sint, sive puncta, ab omni corruptela ita est immunis, ut divina NORMA, canon ac regula sit, ad quam omnes omnino versiones linguarum caeterarum, & praesertim versio Latina vulgata, examinari & emendari debeat. Textus vero N.T. Graecus, in probatis codicibus asservatus, a corruptelis eodem in modum adeo est immunis, ut sit exactissima norma, ad quam omnes versiones & interpretationes examinari & corrigi debeant. Illud prolixe demonstrat D. Glassius lib.1. philol. sacrae tract.1 & 2.
